Sam — quick tech + pricing note to address your three bullets. TL;DR: billing = billed_tokens (input prompt tokens + model output tokens) after any caching/fallback logic; characters are an approximation only. Example math included.

1) Tokens vs characters vs requests
- We tokenize text using a byte-pair encoding; token counts do not equal characters. Rough rule of thumb: 1 token ≈ 3–4 characters for English prose, but that varies with punctuation and non-Latin scripts.
- Billing is per token (not per request). Each API call is analyzed: billed_tokens = prompt_tokens + completion_tokens. If you send 10 requests with 50 prompt tokens each and the model returns 20 tokens each, billed = 10*(50+20) = 700 tokens.

2) Prompt/result caching and billing
- Redwood supports prefix and full-response caching at the serving layer. Behavior depends on cache policy: if the exact request (prompt + routing context) hits a cache and we can return a stored response without running the model, you are not billed for model generation tokens for that hit — only the small bookkeeping overhead (negligible compared to generation).
- If we run a cached lookup that still requires a partial re-generation (e.g., dynamic fields or non-deterministic outputs), billed tokens correspond only to the tokens produced by the model for that request.
- Important: Cache hits are deterministic only if your prompts/context are identical; small template changes change tokenization and miss the cache.

3) Example unit-econ math (hosted list price illustration)
- Hosted price (example): $0.12 per 1k tokens = $120 per 1M tokens. This is the baseline hosted API list price for the model family we discussed.
- Example scenarios for 1M user-visible tokens (to show effective cost with caching/utilization):
  a) No cache: billed tokens = 1,000,000 → cost ≈ $120
  b) 30% full-response cache hit-rate: billed tokens ≈ 700,000 → cost ≈ $84
  c) 60% cache hit-rate: billed tokens ≈ 400,000 → cost ≈ $48

Dedicated / Reserved capacity considerations:
- If you move to Dedicated (reserved capacity) the unit cost reduces but you trade on-commit utilization. With a 12‑month commit and good utilization, effective $/1M can drop into the $40–$90 range depending on model size and utilization profile.

Quick notes on "requests" metric:
- "Requests" is useful for infra sizing (QPS, latency) but not a billing primitive. Two systems with the same number of requests can have very different token bills depending on prompt/output lengths and cache hits.

Attachments: the workbook Priya attached has three worked examples using your sample 400-char prompts and an assumed 1:4 char→token ratio. I also attached a short note on caching policy impacts and how to structure prompts to improve hit-rate (e.g., normalized templates, canonical context ordering).

If helpful I can run a spike on a 48-hour synthetic test to estimate your real-world token conversion and cacheability given a sample of historical prompts.
